extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and humor theory; readers interested in Hobbes's account of laughter
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Thomas Hobbes's 'superiority' (sudden glory) theory to diagnose when laughter is appropriate or what produces it. Focuses on the psychological conditions and exclusions Hobbes sets out for laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining formula: 'sudden glory'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sudden glory is the passion which maketh those grimaces called laughter; and is caused either by some sudden act of their own, that pleaseth them; or by the apprehension of some deformed thing in another, by comparison whereof they suddenly applaud themselves."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Hobbes's canonical statement: laughter is produced by a sudden feeling of glory (eminency/superiority) either from a sudden pleasing act of one's own or by comparing oneself to a deformed/defective other. Use this as the core test for Hobbesian laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glory (feeling of eminency or superiority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter requires a feeling of eminency, superiority, or self-satisfaction (glory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the laugher experiences self-elevation relative to someone or something; mere amusement without self-regard does not satisfy this component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suddenness (abrupt realization)
rubrics_metrics.description: The realization producing glory must be abrupt; gradual recognition does not produce laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter is a brief spike — test whether the sense of superiority arrives suddenly (a 'flash') rather than as a slow accumulation. If the recognition is slow, Hobbes predicts no laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison (to others or to one's former self)
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling arises from comparison either to others' infirmities (defects, deformities, follies) or to one's own former, weaker self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the comparative reference: is the laugher contrasting themselves with another person's failing, or with their own previous weaker state? The comparison is essential for the superiority feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: No present dishonor attached to the comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparison should not bring any present dishonor; men laugh at their past follies 'except they bring with them any present dishonor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the comparison involves present disgrace or shame, the response will not be laughter under Hobbes; check for ongoing dishonor that would convert the reaction into shame rather than glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target with a perceptible defect
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a target with a perceptible defect (intellectual, moral, physical, social) to be laughed at.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the object/joke has a clear flaw or infirmity that can be perceived and compared against the laugher's state; absence of a discernible target undermines Hobbesian laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughterer's awareness of being above the target
rubrics_metrics.description: The laugher must be conscious of being superior to the target in the relevant respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the laugher experiences a sense of being 'above' the target; if the laugher does not feel superior, Hobbes's account does not predict laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spike, not a slow build (brief/sudden nature of laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is short and sudden, like a flash — it is a spike rather than a gradual build.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the temporal profile of the reaction: a quick burst aligns with Hobbes's theory; protracted amusement or slow dawning of humor suggests a different mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: No identification with the target
rubrics_metrics.description: The laugher must not identify with the target; the moment one identifies, laughter stops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for empathy or identification — if the laugher sees themselves in the target, the superiority feeling dissolves and laughter will cease according to Hobbes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological diagnosis of laughers (sign of pusillanimity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavy laughter at others is, for Hobbes, a sign of pusillanimity (small-mindedness); those conscious of few abilities keep themselves in favour by noting others' imperfections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a moral-psychological evaluative criterion: frequent propensity to laugh at others' defects can be taken as evidence of the laugher's insecurity or smallness of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: laughter where no target is lowered
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter at a jest where no target is being lowered is excluded from Hobbesian laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a joke doesn't make someone appear inferior (no comparative lowering), then Hobbes's superiority account does not explain the laughter; seek alternative theories for such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: self-comparison that results in loss (shame, not laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-comparisons where one loses result in shame rather than laughter and so are excluded from Hobbes's account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the comparison makes the self seem worse (present dishonor or loss), classify the emotional response as shame, not laughter under this framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: sympathetic or affectionate laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Sympathetic or affectionate laughter that does not involve a sense of superiority is excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter rooted in affection, bonding, or sympathy should not be explained by superiority; note social/affiliative functions as alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noble exception: laughter at absurdities abstracted from persons
rubrics_metrics.description: It is laudable to laugh at 'absurdities' themselves abstracted from persons, because no individual is being humiliated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the ridicule is directed at abstract absurdity (an idea, situation) rather than a person, Hobbes allows this as acceptable/commendable laughter since no particular person is lowered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic questions for applying the theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions to test whether laughter fits Hobbes's superiority account: Who/what is being looked down upon? Is the laugher's sense of eminence sudden and felt as a spike? Could the joke be told without lowering someone — and would it still work? Does the laughter say more about the laugher's insecurity than about the target?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as a checklist when analyzing an instance of laughter: they operationalize the components and exclusions above and help distinguish Hobbesian cases from other theories of humor.
